## 2. Symbol Analysis

**1. The Numerology of 19:**

#### 1 + 9 = 10 = 1

In numerology, 19 breaks down into 1 and 9, which add up to 10, and 10 ultimately reduces back to 1. This process actually conveys the most touching meaning of The Sun card: after completing a full circle of life, you return to your original intention—but this time, you come back carrying light.

1 represents a beginning, the child riding a white horse, smiling without any burden—symbolizing the purest self, as free as The Fool, as full of potential as The Magician.

9 represents an ending, the wisdom gained by the Hermit after walking a long path with a lantern, the inner completeness achieved after experiencing confusion, pain, and doubt.

When 1 meets 9, it’s not a return to the starting point but an upgraded restart. You are no longer the naive child but someone who sees through the world yet still chooses to believe. This joy is not because you have never been hurt, but because you have been hurt, feared, and lost—and finally found yourself through your own light.

![Tarot illustration](https://internal-api-drive-stream.feishu.cn/space/api/box/stream/download/authcode/?code=OGU0NzVkNTY0YTgzYjZhZWE5ZWUzYWYyODAwMTdjMjNfMDM0NzVlZjA5MTQzNzM0MjliZTc2NDY3ZGE1ODZmMmVfSUQ6NzYyMjMzMzE2MzQ5NDM5NTA2OV8xNzgyMTgxNDg2OjE3ODIyNjc4ODZfVjM)

The number 10 corresponds to the Wheel of Fortune, which further emphasizes that every ending is the beginning of a new cycle. So the “1” in The Sun card is a higher-dimensional 1—clear, resolute, and completely free.

The Sun card (19) follows directly after The Moon card (18).

The Moon represents midnight: foggy, shadows flickering, even doubting oneself;

The Sun represents noon: the sky is clear, everything is distinct, even the dust in the corner is exposed.

**2. Belongs to the Fire Element**

In Tarot, The Sun card belongs to the fire element, but it’s not the kind of fire that burns everything down. It’s like the midday sun—warm, bright, and full of vitality. It neither attacks nor hides; it simply shines steadily on all things, bringing energy, health, and clarity. This fire radiates outward: your talents are seen, your efforts recognized, and your heart no longer hides but naturally reveals itself.

**3. Astrological Correspondence: The Sun**

In astrology, this card directly corresponds to the Sun itself.

The Sun represents the “true you”: confident, resolute, knowing who you are without relying on others’ judgments to confirm your worth. It also symbolizes the most flourishing state in life—career success, clear relationships, and a full spirit, everything moving at the “zenith” of its rhythm. This is not accidental luck but the light you live after passing through darkness and mist.

**4. Hebrew Letter: Forehead or Head**

In the Kabbalah system, The Sun card corresponds to the Hebrew letter Resh (ר), meaning “head” or “forehead.”

This is very interesting—the forehead is where we open our eyes to see the world, representing clear consciousness and the light of reason. Compared to the previous card, The Moon, which corresponds to the “back of the head,” symbolizing the subconscious and instinct, The Sun card represents a fully awakened state: no longer deceived by illusions, no longer doubting oneself, but facing reality and seeing the truth clearly.

Just like the sunflowers on the card that always turn toward the sun, Resh reminds you to turn your attention to the light, aiming at the direction you truly believe in. The “head” also means beginning and leadership—you are no longer a passive follower but someone ready to steer your own life.

Therefore, the joy of The Sun card is grounded; its brightness is something cherished after experiencing darkness.

## 3. Case Studies

### The Sun Card and Ding Zhen

In the journey of the Fool, The Sun card represents the moment after all experiences when one reaches a life highlight but still maintains a childlike heart, returning to the purest and most authentic state.

In the Tarot deck, The Sun card is arguably the most positive and uplifting card. It represents success, truth revealed, the clearing of gloom, and a vigorous life force with a clear sense of direction. It’s like a triumphant return after a long journey.

The image on this card shows a naked child riding a white horse, laughing under the sunlight. This expresses that when you overcome all obstacles and return to your purest, freest self, that state is “The Sun.”

Ding Zhen’s story fits this card perfectly.

In 2020, a photographer encountered 19-year-old Ding Zhen in Litang, Sichuan. In the video, his eyes are clear, his smile shy, his face flushed from the plateau, and he only says “hello” in Tibetan. Netizens said his eyes held no desire, only snow mountains and lakes. Isn’t this exactly the “naked child” in The Sun card? He shed all social masks, leaving only the most authentic existence.

The viral video shows him riding his white horse “Pearl” galloping across the grassland, the wind lifting his clothes, his smile radiant. The white horse symbolizes purity and freedom; his harmony with the horse shows the unity between humans and nature. This is like the child on the card riding the horse—not conquering but dancing together; not performing but living.

After becoming famous, he became Litang’s tourism ambassador, appeared on magazine covers, and even participated in the Spring Festival Gala. Facing sudden fame and fortune, he did not hype himself or over-commercialize. Despite being crowned with the “wreath” of fame and fortune, he chose to return to Litang, guarding his hometown and original heart. This is exactly what The Sun card wants to tell us: success is not the end but allows you to be freer to be yourself.

Because of him, Litang’s tourism searches surged, and the local economy genuinely benefited. He promoted employment among Tibetan youth, spread ethnic culture, and declined many high-paying but unsuitable endorsements. In the complex entertainment industry, he is like a fresh breeze, relying on authenticity rather than persona. The light of The Sun card never blinds but dispels gloom and awakens hope.

Now, at 24, he still shares daily life on social media—feeding lambs, riding horses, eating tsampa. Facing criticism, he does not argue but proves with actions: I am still that boy from Litang. His smile remains the same—clean, shy, and without calculation.

This is the most precious part of The Sun card: after the noise, returning still a child.
